summary: Describes TCP SYN flooding attacks, which were well known at the time, and the various countermeasures with their tradeoffs. It archives explanations of the attack and common defenses for implementers and administrators, without making standards-level recommendations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone rings a doorbell thousands of times and runs away, so the host keeps waiting. This explains that trick and ways to handle it.

questions: what is a tcp syn flood
how to mitigate syn flooding attacks
subtitle: The attack that exploits TCP connection setup and proven defenses against it

tldr.problem: A TCP server has a limited queue for half-open connections during the three-way handshake. An attacker can flood the server with SYN packets using spoofed source addresses, filling the queue with bogus connections so legitimate clients cannot connect.
tldr.mechanism: The attacker sends SYN segments with spoofed source addresses that will not reply to SYN-ACKs. Each SYN fills a slot in the backlog queue. Defenses include filtering spoofed packets, shortening timeouts, SYN cache (minimal state per half-open), and SYN cookies (stateless, encoding connection info in sequence numbers).
tldr.outcome: The attack has been known since 1994 and publicly disclosed in 1996. Most modern operating systems implement one or more defenses. SYN cache and SYN cookies are the most effective end-host solutions, though SYN cookies have compatibility tradeoffs with some TCP options.

today: RFC 4987 documents a well-known attack that remains relevant. Most modern TCP implementations now include defenses (SYN cache or SYN cookies). The techniques are mature and widely deployed. However, the attack is still possible against poorly configured systems and newer variants (SYN floods from botnets) remain a concern. The document remains the authoritative archive of the attack mechanism and common countermeasures.

sections.title: The Attack and Its History
sections.content:
The TCP SYN flooding attack exploits the connection establishment procedure. When a TCP server is in the LISTEN state, a SYN segment causes the server to allocate state (a Transmission Control Block or TCB) and transition to SYN-RECEIVED state, waiting for a SYN-ACK to complete the handshake. The server allocates memory for each half-open connection and limits the total number of such states to some backlog value.

An attacker floods the server with SYN segments using spoofed source IP addresses that will never send replies. Each SYN consumes a slot in the backlog, preventing legitimate connection attempts from being processed. The attack was discovered as early as 1994 by Cheswick and Bellovin but publicized widely in September 1996 through Phrack Magazine and the CERT advisory CA-96.21. In practice attacks have been observed on real networks, causing major outages to ISP mail servers.

The document focuses on attacks against individual servers or services, not bulk network capacity attacks, and archives explanation and common defenses for TCP implementers and administrators without standardizing any single solution.
sections.plainLanguage: A TCP server waiting for connections saves information about each half-finished handshake. An attacker sends many fake SYN messages that claim to come from addresses that will not answer back. The server wastes its memory on these fake connections and runs out of space for real ones. Legitimate users get rejected and cannot connect.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
The effectiveness of a SYN flood depends on three parameters. Barrage size: the number of SYN segments sent must exceed the backlog. Typical default backlogs range from a few dozen to a few hundred, so attacking with roughly the backlog size is efficient. Barrage frequency: TCP implementations have a timeout (often 75 seconds) after which half-open TCBs are reclaimed. If the timeout expires before new barrages arrive, the queue clears and legitimate connections become possible. Attackers time new barrages to refill the queue before reclamation. IP address selection: spoofed addresses must be unresponsive to SYN-ACK responses. If the addresses are real hosts on the Internet, those hosts will send TCP RST (reset) segments that immediately free the TCB slot, defeating the attack. Effective attacks use either a list of unresponsive addresses or compromised hosts (a botnet) that suppress their normal response to SYN-ACKs.

The RFC notes that in practice attacks may use botnets instead of spoofing, and attack traffic may be continuous rather than in discrete barrages, as long as the arrival rate of new SYNs exceeds the rate of TCB reclamation.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacker must send enough fake SYNs to fill the queue. If the server stops waiting after 75 seconds, the attacker must send more SYNs before the queue empties. The attacker uses fake return addresses that will not answer back, or fake computers under the attacker's control. Without these tricks, the real address owners would send reset signals that free up the queue space.

sections.title: Common Defense Techniques
sections.content:
Filtering: Ingress filtering (RFCs 2827, 3013, 3704) prevents spoofed packets from leaving an attacker's network. This is highly effective but requires global deployment and is not reliable against botnets or multihomed attackers.

Increasing backlog: Simply enlarging the backlog is ineffective because larger backlogs require more memory and the search algorithms of some TCP stacks do not scale well past a few hundred entries.

Reducing SYN-RECEIVED timeout: Shorter timeouts free up queue space sooner but hurt legitimate slow clients and only linearly increase the required attacker traffic rate.

SYN Cache: Instead of allocating a full TCB on the first SYN, a SYN cache stores minimal state in a hash table indexed by secret bits derived from the SYN. When the ACK arrives, state is reconstructed if the hash still matches. This bounds both memory and CPU usage. SYN cache was first implemented in BSD/OS in 1996 and is now in FreeBSD, NetBSD, and OpenBSD. Evaluation shows legitimate connection time is slightly longer under attack but scaling is linear with attack size, not quadratic.

SYN Cookies: This technique allocates zero state on receipt of a SYN. The server encodes most required state into the sequence number of the SYN-ACK, including an MSS value (2 bits), a time-dependent counter (5 bits), and a server secret (24 bits). If an ACK arrives, the server reconstructs state from the acknowledging sequence number and validates it against recent counter values. SYN cookies are stateless but incompatible with some TCP options like window scaling and SACK unless special care is taken. They are typically not enabled by default and only activated during high attack load.

Firewalls and proxies: These complete the three-way handshake with the attacker and proxy the connection to the protected server, shifting the burden from the end host to the firewall. This may introduce other issues.
sections.plainLanguage: One defense is to refuse to accept packets from fake addresses at the edge of the network. Another is to forget about half-open connections faster, though this hurts slow real clients. The best end-host defenses use clever tricks: save just a tiny bit of information in a hash table instead of allocating full memory (SYN cache), or encode all the state needed in the SYN-ACK sequence number and throw away the information, reconstructing it only if a real ACK comes back (SYN cookies). A firewall can handle the handshake itself and then pass the real connection to the server.

sections.title: Analysis and Deployment
sections.content:
Among end-host defenses, SYN cache and SYN cookies are the only truly effective solutions. Increasing backlog and reducing timeouts are ineffective. SYN cache uses more memory than SYN cookies but has no TCP option compatibility issues and is safe to enable by default. SYN cookies save memory but limit TCP option negotiation (window scaling, SACK) and are typically not enabled by default.

A newer hybrid SYN cookie technique in FreeBSD leverages the Timestamp option to store additional state bits, allowing better negotiation of options while remaining stateless. However, this requires the client to send a Timestamp option.

SYN cache was first implemented in 1996 by Dave Borman at BSDi and is the basis for implementations in later BSD variants. Linux 2.6.5 includes a SYN cookie implementation encoding 8 MSS values. Windows 2000 and later added a configurable SYN attack protection feature that reduces SYN-ACK retransmissions and delays route cache entry creation under attack. Some vendors sell commercial firewall products that proxy connections.

The discovery of the SYN flooding vulnerability taught protocol designers a lesson: newer protocols like SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) and HIP (Host Identity Protocol) incorporate stateless or puzzle-based connection setup to avoid allocating resources before verifying the initiator's address.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-world testing shows SYN cache works well and is safe to always use. SYN cookies work best when clients support the Timestamp option. Most operating systems now have at least one of these defenses built in. New protocols designed since the SYN flood attack was discovered use different handshake designs that do not have this problem.

sections.title: Security and Conclusions
sections.content: The SYN flooding attack details are well known and exploit tools have been widely available for years. Documenting the attack and defenses in this RFC does not introduce new risks but rather educates TCP implementers and administrators about widely deployed mitigation techniques. Many modern operating systems implement SYN cache or SYN cookies by default or can enable them easily. The document concludes that systems should provide some form of end-host defense, as global deployment of ingress filtering cannot be assumed. The publication of this RFC may increase robustness by encouraging use of available mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the industry already knows about this attack and how to defend against it. This document just puts the knowledge in one place so engineers and operators can understand the defenses and use them effectively. The attack has become less devastating because most systems now have built-in protections.
